en: Thus have I heard— *Majjhima Nikāya 12: Mahāsīhanādasutta* (The Great Lion’s Roar Discourse) Thus have I heard: [One day] the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of assemblies. What four? The assembly of nobles, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, and the assembly of ascetics. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of assemblies. Now, bhikkhus, when a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of devas and humans, an awakened one, a Blessed One; and when he teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and reveals a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure—then, bhikkhus, the assembly of nobles, having heard that Dhamma, gains faith in the Tathāgata.

Having gained faith, they approach him. Having approached, they pay homage to him and sit down to one side. As they sit there, the Tathāgata instructs, urges, rouses, and gladdens them with a talk on the Dhamma. Being instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the Tathāgata with a talk on the Dhamma, they delight in that Dhamma and embrace it. They become his disciples, following his instructions and honoring him as their teacher. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble assembly. And how, bhikkhus, is the assembly of brahmins... the assembly of householders... the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata? Here, bhikkhus, when a Tathāgata has arisen in the world... and when he teaches the Dhamma... then the assembly of ascetics, having heard that Dhamma, gains faith in the Tathāgata. Having gained faith, they approach him. Having approached, they pay homage to him and sit down to one side. As they sit there, the Tathāgata instructs, urges, rouses, and gladdens them with a talk on the Dhamma. Being instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the Tathāgata with a talk on the Dhamma, they delight in that Dhamma and embrace it. They become his disciples, following his instructions and honoring him as their teacher. This, bhikkhus, is called the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of assemblies. Among these four kinds of assemblies, bhikkhus, the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata is declared to be foremost, best, preeminent, supreme, and the most excellent. [The Buddha then proceeded to describe the various qualities of the Tathāgata, such as his mastery over the four bases of psychic power, his possession of the six direct knowledges, and his realization of the destruction of the taints. “Bhikkhus, when a Tathāgata has arisen in the world... and when he teaches the Dhamma... then the assembly of nobles... the assembly of brahmins... the assembly of householders... the assembly of ascetics, having heard that Dhamma, gains faith in the Tathāgata. Having gained faith, they approach him. Having approached, they pay homage to him and sit down to one side. As they sit there, the Tathāgata instructs, urges, rouses, and gladdens them with a talk on the Dhamma. Being instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the Tathāgata with a talk on the Dhamma, they delight in that Dhamma and embrace it. They become his disciples, following his instructions and honoring him as their teacher. This, bhikkhus, is called the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata. Among these four kinds of assemblies, bhikkhus, the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata is declared to be foremost, best, preeminent, supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the footprints, the footprint of the elephant is declared to be foremost, best, preeminent, supreme, and the most excellent; so too, among these four kinds of assemblies, the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata is declared to be foremost, best, preeminent, supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the small animals, the lion, the king of beasts, is declared to be foremost... so too, among these four kinds of assemblies, the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata is declared to be foremost... Just as, bhikkhus, among all the animals, the royal bull elephant is declared to be foremost... so too, among these four kinds of assemblies, the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata is declared to be foremost... Just as, bhikkhus, among all the birds, the golden-winged garuḍa is declared to be foremost... so too, among these four kinds of assemblies, the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata is declared to be foremost... Just as, bhikkhus, among all the constellations, the moon is declared to be foremost... so too, among these four kinds of assemblies, the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata is declared to be foremost... Just as, bhikkhus, among all the luminaries, the sun is declared to be foremost... so too, among these four kinds of assemblies, the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata is declared to be foremost... Just as, bhikkhus, among all the great rivers, the ocean is declared to be foremost... so too, among these four kinds of assemblies, the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata is declared to be foremost... Just as, bhikkhus, among all the mountains, Mount Sineru is declared to be foremost... so too, among these four kinds of assemblies, the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata is declared to be foremost, best, preeminent, supreme, and the most excellent. [The Buddha then continued with a series of similes regarding the Tathāgata’s mastery over the four bases of psychic power, his possession of the six direct knowledges, and his realization of the destruction of the taints. “Bhikkhus, when a Tathāgata has arisen in the world... and when he teaches the Dhamma... then the assembly of nobles... the assembly of brahmins... the assembly of householders... the assembly of ascetics, having heard that Dhamma, gains faith in the Tathāgata. Having gained faith, they approach him. Having approached, they pay homage to him and sit down to one side. As they sit there, the Tathāgata instructs, urges, rouses, and gladdens them with a talk on the Dhamma. Being instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the Tathāgata with a talk on the Dhamma, they delight in that Dhamma and embrace it. They become his disciples, following his instructions and honoring him as their teacher. This, bhikkhus, is called the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata.

Among these four kinds of assemblies, bhikkhus, the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata is declared to be foremost, best, preeminent, supreme, and the most excellent. When a Tathāgata has arisen in the world... and when he teaches the Dhamma... then the assembly of nobles... the assembly of brahmins... the assembly of householders... the assembly of ascetics, having heard that Dhamma, gains faith in the Tathāgata. Having gained faith, they approach him. Having approached, they pay homage to him and sit down to one side. As they sit there, the Tathāgata instructs, urges, rouses, and gladdens them with a talk on the Dhamma. Being instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the Tathāgata with a talk on the Dhamma, they delight in that Dhamma and embrace it. They become his disciples, following his instructions and honoring him as their teacher. This, bhikkhus, is called the assembly of ascetics well-disciplined by the Tathāgata. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī, outside the city in the grove of Aparapura.
Now at that time Sunakkhatta, the son of the Licchavis, had recently departed from this Dhamma and Vinaya.
He was speaking these words in an assembly at Vesālī:
“The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman state, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
The ascetic Gotama teaches a doctrine hammered out by reasoning, following his own line of inquiry, based on his own inspiration;
and that for which his doctrine is taught leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.”
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Sāriputta dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms.
There he heard Sunakkhatta, the son of the Licchavis, speaking these words in the assembly at Vesālī:
"The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman state, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of a noble one."
“The ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma that is hammered out by reasoning, followed by inquiry, and based on his own inspired intuition.
And for whatever purpose this Dhamma is taught, it leads one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.
Then, having walked for alms in Vesālī and returned from his almsround after the meal, the Venerable Sāriputta—
He approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son has not long since departed from this Dhamma and Vinaya.”
Thus, in the assembly at Vesālī, he speaks these words:
“The ascetic Gotama possesses no superhuman state, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
The ascetic Gotama teaches a doctrine that is hammered out by reasoning, followed by inquiry, and based on his own ingenuity.”
“And for whatever purpose the Dhamma has been taught to him, it leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.
“For this foolish man Sunakkhatta is angry, Sāriputta;
and it was out of anger that he spoke these words.”
“Sāriputta, when the foolish man Sunakkhatta says, ‘I shall speak dispraise,’ he actually speaks only praise of the Tathāgata. For this, Sāriputta, is praise of the Tathāgata:
that one might say, ‘For whatever purpose the Dhamma has been taught by him, it leads the practitioner who puts it into practice to the complete destruction of suffering.’”
Indeed, Sāriputta, even this inference regarding the Dhamma will not occur to the foolish man Sunakkhatta concerning me:

“In such a way is that Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Indeed, Sāriputta, even this inference regarding the Dhamma will not occur to the foolish man Sunakkhatta concerning me.
‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: he experiences various kinds of psychic power—he, being one, becomes many;
being many, he becomes one; he appears and disappears; he passes through walls, enclosures, and mountains unhindered, as if through space;
he dives in and out of the earth, as if it were water.’
"In water; he walks upon water without breaking the surface, just as on earth; he travels through the air cross-legged, just like a winged bird;
with his hand he touches and strokes even the sun and moon, so powerful and majestic;
and he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world."
Indeed, Sāriputta, this too shall not occur to the foolish man Sunakkhatta as a logical inference regarding me:
‘In such a way the Blessed One, with the purified divine ear-element, surpassing that of humans, hears both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near.
Indeed, Sāriputta, this too shall not occur to the foolish man Sunakkhatta as a logical inference regarding me:
‘Such indeed is that Blessed One: he understands the minds of other beings and other persons, having encompassed them with his own mind—
he understands a mind affected by lust as “a mind affected by lust,” and he understands a mind free from lust as “a mind free from lust”;’
He understands a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred,
and he understands a mind free from hatred as a mind free from hatred;
he understands a deluded mind as a deluded mind.
He understands a mind free from delusion as "a mind free from delusion";
he understands a contracted mind as "a contracted mind," and he understands a scattered mind as "a scattered mind."
He understands a vast mind as a vast mind,
or he understands a non-vast mind as a non-vast mind;
or he understands a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind.
Or he understands an unsurpassed mind as an unsurpassed mind;
or he understands a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind,
and an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind.
‘He understands a liberated mind as a liberated mind,
and he understands an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.

Moreover, Sāriputta, there are these ten powers of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
What are the ten?
Here, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible.
Insofar, Sāriputta, as the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible...
This too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel. Furthermore, Sāriputta,
the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the result of the undertaking of kamma— past, future, and present— in terms of its basis and its cause.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, when the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the result of the undertaking of kamma— past, future, and present— in terms of its basis and its cause, this too, Sāriputta, is a power of the Tathāgata;
by relying on which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, and roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies.
He sets in motion the Wheel of Brahma.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the practice that leads everywhere.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the practice that leads everywhere—this too, Sāriputta...
Sāriputta, the Tathāgata possesses a power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel. Furthermore, Sāriputta,
the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the world with its many and diverse elements.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, that the Tathāgata understands the world with its many and diverse elements as it really is—
this too, Sāriputta, is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the diversity of the inclinations of beings.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the diversity of the inclinations of beings—
this too, Sāriputta, is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata stands in the place of the bull.
He claims [the place], he roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and he sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the degree of the faculties of other beings, of other persons.
That too, Sāriputta, is how the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the degree of the faculties of other beings, of other persons.

He understands this; Sāriputta, this too is a Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the defilement, the cleansing, and the emergence regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, when the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the defilement, the cleansing, and the emergence regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments— this too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata’s power,
by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place of leadership, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past abodes,
that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births,
twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births...
Even for a hundred thousand births, or many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, or many aeons of both contraction and expansion, [he recollects:
"In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I arose elsewhere; and there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, and such experience of pleasure and pain."
‘Having had such a lifespan, passing away from there, he has reappeared here. Thus, with its aspects and particulars, he recollects his manifold past abodes.
Sāriputta, that the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past abodes, such as one [life]...
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... [as before] ...thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.

This, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans,
the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and being reborn— low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma:
"These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct of body, misconduct of speech..."
Endowed with misconduct of mind, revilers of the noble ones, possessing wrong view, and undertaking actions based on wrong view,
these beings, upon the breakup of the body after death, have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But these worthy beings, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind—
‘...endowed with these qualities, not reviling the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking kamma based on right view,
they— upon the breakup of the body, after death— have reappeared in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye,
purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn— low and high, beautiful and ugly.

He understands beings as they pass away and reappear, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, according to their kamma. Sāriputta, when with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and reappearing— inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, according to their kamma.
He understands beings thus: "These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, possessed of misconduct in mind;
they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell. Or these..."
‘But these worthy beings, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, endowed with good conduct of mind,
not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking actions based on right view—
on the dissolution of the body, after death, have reappeared in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the purified divine eye...

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their karma. This, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata;
by relying on this power, the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, and roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies.
He sets in motion the Wheel of Brahma.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, with the destruction of the taints, the Tathāgata realizes for himself through direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein.
That too, Sāriputta, is because the Tathāgata, with the destruction of the taints... [realizes] the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life.
Having realized the Dhamma for himself through direct higher knowledge, he enters upon and dwells in it— this too, Sāriputta,
is a Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
"These, Sāriputta, are the ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessed of which a Tathāgata claims his place of leadership, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Sāriputta, if anyone were to say of me, who thus knows and thus sees:
‘There is no superhuman state, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, for the ascetic Gotama;'"
“‘The ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma that is hammered out by reasoning,

followed by inquiry, and based on his own inspired insight’— if one does not abandon such speech, does not abandon such a mind, and does not relinquish such a view, then, Sāriputta, one will be placed in hell as if carried there.

Just as a bhikkhu who is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom might attain final knowledge (aññā) in this very life, even so, Sāriputta, I declare this to be the case.”
Without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that mind, and without relinquishing that view, one is placed in hell just as if carried there.

"Sāriputta, there are these four grounds of self-confidence belonging to a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
What are the four?"
‘While you claim to be a perfectly awakened Buddha, these things have not been fully realized by you.
In this regard, Sāriputta, I do not see any ground for anyone in the world— whether a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else— to rightfully challenge me thus.
Not perceiving any such ground for this, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained self-confidence:

“If anyone—whether a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world—should challenge me in accordance with the Dhamma, saying, ‘While you claim to be one whose taints are destroyed, these taints are not yet destroyed in you,’ I see no basis for that. This is the ground [for my confidence].
“Sāriputta, I do not perceive such a sign.
Not perceiving this sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained self-confidence.
As for those things called ‘obstructive states,’ they are not capable of being obstructive for one who indulges in them. In that regard—
“Sāriputta, I do not see any ground on which anyone in the world— whether a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else at all—
could rightfully challenge me. Seeing no such ground, Sāriputta,
I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained self-confidence.”
"Moreover, for whomsoever this Dhamma has been taught by you, it does not lead that practitioner to the complete destruction of suffering.
In this regard, Sāriputta, I do not see any ground on which a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world could rightfully challenge me.
Not perceiving even this sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained intrepidity.

These, Sāriputta, are the four grounds of self-confidence of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Sāriputta, whoever should speak thus of me while knowing me thus and seeing me thus: [omitted].
‘The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman states, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones;

the ascetic Gotama teaches a doctrine hammered out by reasoning, following his own inquiry, and based on his own ingenuity’—if one does not abandon that speech, does not abandon that thought, and does not relinquish that view, Sāriputta, one is deposited in hell just as if carried there.

"Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu who is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom might attain final knowledge in this very life, even so, Sāriputta, do I say it is with this person.
Without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that mind, and without relinquishing that view, he is placed in hell as if carried there.
There are, Sāriputta, these eight assemblies."

Which eight? The assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of ascetics, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three Gods, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā—
these, Sāriputta, are the eight assemblies.
"Endowed with these four grounds of self-confidence, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata approaches and enters deeply into these eight assemblies.
Indeed, Sāriputta, I recall having approached many hundreds of assemblies of khattiyas;
there too I have previously sat together, conversed, and engaged in discussion."
"In this regard, Sāriputta, I do not perceive any ground for thinking, 'Fear or trepidation will overcome me.
Not perceiving such a ground, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained self-confidence.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, I recall many hundreds of assemblies of brahmins... [and so on]."
...the assembly of householders ...
the assembly of ascetics ...
the assembly of the Four Great Kings ...
They have approached the assembly of the Thirty-three,
the assembly of Māra,
and the assembly of Brahmā.

In that regard, Sāriputta, I do not perceive any ground for thinking: "Fear or trepidation will come upon me there, as I have previously sat together with them, conversed with them, and engaged in discussion with them.
Not perceiving such a ground, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained self-confidence.
Sāriputta, whoever should speak thus of me—knowing me as I am and seeing me as I am:
“The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman states, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones;

the ascetic Gotama teaches a doctrine hammered out by reasoning, following his own line of inquiry, and based on his own ingenuity,” then, Sāriputta, unless he abandons that speech, abandons that thought, and relinquishes that view, he will be placed in hell as if carried there.
"Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom might attain final knowledge in this very life, so too, Sāriputta, I say this:
without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that mind, and without relinquishing that view, one is placed in hell just as if carried there.
There are, Sāriputta, these four modes of birth."
Which four?
The egg-born birth, the womb-born birth, the moisture-born birth, and the spontaneously born birth.
And what, Sāriputta, is the egg-born birth?
Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born having broken out of an eggshell—
this, Sāriputta, is called the egg-born mode of birth.
And what, Sāriputta, is the womb-born mode of birth?
Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born having broken through the membrane of the womb—
this, Sāriputta, is called the womb-born mode of birth (jalābu-jā yoni).
And what, Sāriputta, is the moisture-born mode of birth (saṁsedajā yoni)?
“Sāriputta, those beings who are born in rotten fish, or born in putrid corpses, or born in rotten bean curd, or born in cesspools,
or born in slime— this, Sāriputta, is called the moisture-born mode of birth.
And what, Sāriputta, is the spontaneously born mode of birth?”
Devas, denizens of hell, certain humans, and certain beings in the states of deprivation—
this, Sāriputta, is called the womb of spontaneous birth.
These, Sāriputta, are the four wombs.
Sāriputta, whoever should say of me—while I am known and seen by them in this way:
“The ascetic Gotama possesses no superhuman states, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones;

the ascetic Gotama teaches a doctrine hammered out by reasoning, following his own inquiry, and based on his own ingenuity”—if they do not abandon that speech, do not abandon that thought, and do not relinquish that view, then, as if carried there, they will be placed in hell.

"Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu who is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom might attain final knowledge in this very life, so too, Sāriputta, I say it is with this person.
Without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that mind, and without relinquishing that view, he is placed in hell just like one who has been carried there.
There are, Sāriputta, these five destinations."
Which five?
Hell, the animal realm, the sphere of hungry ghosts, human beings, and devas.
Sāriputta, I understand hell, the path leading to hell, and the practice leading to hell;
And I understand how one who has practiced accordingly, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell.
Sāriputta, I understand the animal realm, the path leading to the animal realm, and the practice leading to the animal realm;
and I understand how one who has practiced accordingly, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in the animal realm.
“Sāriputta, I understand the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya), the path leading to the realm of hungry ghosts, and the practice leading to the realm of hungry ghosts;
and I understand how one who has practiced accordingly is reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts after the breakup of the body, after death.
Sāriputta, I understand human beings, the path leading to the world of humans, and the practice leading to the world of humans.”
I understand how one who has practiced accordingly is reborn among human beings after the breakup of the body, after death;
and I, Sāriputta, understand the devas, the path leading to the world of the devas, and the practice leading to the world of the devas;
and I understand how one who has practiced accordingly is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, after the breakup of the body, after death.
“Sāriputta, I understand Nibbāna, I understand the path leading to Nibbāna, and I understand the practice leading to Nibbāna;

and I also understand how, by practicing accordingly, one realizes for oneself through direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having exhausted the taints, and dwells therein.
Here, Sāriputta, with my mind I encompass the mind of a certain person and understand thus:”
"Furthermore, this person has practiced, conducted himself, and entered upon that path such that, with the breakup of the body after death, he will be reborn in a state of deprivation,
a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell. Later, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see him—
with the breakup of the body after death— reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell, experiencing exclusively suffering."
Experiencing sharp and bitter feelings.
It is just as if, Sāriputta, there were a charcoal pit deeper than a man’s height, filled with glowing coals, devoid of smoke.
Then a person might come along, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, parched, and thirsty, traveling along a one-way path leading directly toward that very charcoal pit.
A man with sight, seeing him, would say:
"This person is practicing in such a way, behaving in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that he will surely come to this very pit of glowing embers.
And at a later time, one might see him fallen into that pit of glowing embers, experiencing sensations that are exclusively painful, intense, and bitter.
In the same way, Sāriputta, here I encompass the mind of a certain person with my own mind and understand:

"This person is practicing in such a way, conducting himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, with the breakup of the body after death, he will reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
Then, at a later time, I see him with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans...
"With the breakup of the body, after death, he has been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell, experiencing exclusively painful,
sharp, and bitter sensations. But here, Sāriputta,
having encompassed with my own mind the mind of a certain person, I understand thus:
"In such a way this person has practiced, in such a way he conducts himself, and has ascended upon that path, that after the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the animal realm.

Then, at a later time, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I see him—after the breakup of the body, after death—reborn in the animal realm, experiencing painful, racking, piercing feelings.
It is just as if, Sāriputta, there were a cesspool more than a man’s height deep, full of excrement."
Then a man might come along, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, thirsty, and parched, traveling by a one-way path directed straight toward that very cesspool.
A man with sight, seeing him, would say:
"This person is proceeding in such a way, acting in such a manner, and has entered upon such a path that he will surely come to this very cesspool."
Suppose one were to see him at a later time fallen into that cesspool, experiencing painful, sharp, and bitter sensations.
In the same way, Sāriputta, here I encompass the mind of a certain person with my own mind and understand:
"This person is practicing in such a way, conducting himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path, that with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the animal realm."

Then, on a later occasion, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see him reborn in the animal realm after the breakup of the body, after death, experiencing painful, sharp, and bitter feelings.
But here, Sāriputta, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I understand:

"This person is practicing in such a way, conducting himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path, that after the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the sphere of hungry ghosts."

Then, on a later occasion, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see him—after the breakup of the body, after death—reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*), experiencing feelings of great suffering.
Sāriputta, it is just as if there were a tree growing on uneven ground, with sparse leaves and foliage and a mottled shade.
Then a man, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, parched, and thirsty, might come along a one-way path and direct his attention toward that very tree.
A man with sight, seeing him, would say:
"In such a way this person has practiced, in such a way he conducts himself, and he has set out upon that path, that he will come to this very tree.
And at a later time, one might see him sitting or lying down in the shade of that tree, experiencing feelings of great suffering.
In the same way, Sāriputta, here I encompass the mind of a certain person with my own mind and understand:

"This person is practicing in such a way, conducting himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path, that with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts.

Then, at a later time, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I see him, with the breakup of the body, after death, reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, experiencing feelings full of suffering.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, here I encompass the mind of a certain person with my own mind and understand:
"This person is practicing in such a way, conducting himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, with the breakup of the body after death, he will be reborn among human beings.

Then, at a later time, I see him—with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans—reborn among human beings with the breakup of the body after death, experiencing feelings that are mostly pleasant.
"Just as, Sāriputta, there might be a tree growing on level ground with thick foliage and leaves, casting a deep shade.
Then a person, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, parched, and thirsty, might come along a one-way path directed toward that very tree.
A man with sight, seeing him, would say this:"
‘This person, so practicing, so conducting himself, and having entered upon that path, will come to this very tree.
Then, at a later time, one might see him sitting or lying down in the shade of that tree, experiencing feelings of great ease.
In the same way, Sāriputta, here I encompass the mind of a certain person with my own mind and understand it thus:
"In this way, this person has practiced, conducts himself, and has entered upon that path such that, with the breakup of the body after death, he will be reborn among human beings.
Later on, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see him—with the breakup of the body after death—reborn among human beings, experiencing feelings of great happiness.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, here I understand a certain person by encompassing his mind with my own mind thus:

‘This person has practiced in such a way, conducts himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, with the breakup of the body after death, he will reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.

Later on, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I see him, with the breakup of the body after death, reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, experiencing exclusively pleasant feelings.
"Just as, Sāriputta, there might be a palace, and in it a gabled chamber plastered within and without, protected from the wind, with its door-panels closed and its windows shuttered.
In it there would be a couch spread with a woolen cover, a white woolen cover, a flowered woolen cover, and a choice spread of antelope hide, with a canopy above and red bolsters at both ends.
Then a man might come, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, weary, parched, and thirsty, traveling along a one-way path directed toward that very palace."
A man with sight, seeing him, would say:
"In such a way this person has practiced, in such a way he conducts himself, and he has set out upon such a path that he will surely come to this very palace.
And at a later time, one might see him sitting or lying down in that palace, in that gabled chamber, on that couch, experiencing exclusively pleasant feelings.
In the same way, Sāriputta, here I encompass the mind of a certain person with my own mind and understand:

"This person is practicing in such a way, conducting himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, with the breakup of the body after death, he will reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
Then, at a later time, I see him with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, having reappeared in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, experiencing exclusively pleasant feelings.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, here I understand a certain person by encompassing his mind with my own mind:
"This person is practicing in such a way, conducting himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path,
that through the destruction of the taints, he will realize for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom."
‘He will enter and dwell therein.

Then, at a later time, I see him— having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom through the destruction of the taints, and having entered and dwelt therein— experiencing feelings that are exclusively pleasant.
"Just as, Sāriputta, there might be a lotus pond with clear water, sweet water, cool water, white water, with easy access, and delightful;
and not far from it, a dense grove of trees.
Then a man might come along, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, parched, and thirsty, traveling by a path that goes in only one direction, aiming for that very lotus pond."
A man with keen sight, seeing him, would say:
"That person is practicing in such a way, conducts himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that he will surely come to this very lotus pond.
And at a later time, one might see him having descended into that lotus pond, bathed, and drunk.
Having allayed every distress, fatigue, and fever, and having emerged [from concentration], I see him sitting or lying down in that forest grove,
experiencing exclusively pleasant feelings.
In the same way, Sāriputta, I here understand a certain person by encompassing his mind with my own mind thus:
‘This person is practicing in such a way, conducts himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that,
through the destruction of the taints, he will realize for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,
and having attained it, will dwell therein.’

Then, at a later time, I see him— having realized for himself through direct knowledge in this very life, having attained and dwelled in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom through the destruction of the taints— experiencing feelings that are exclusively pleasant.
These, Sāriputta, are the five destinations.
Sāriputta, if anyone were to say of me, who knows and sees thus:
“The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman states, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones;
the ascetic Gotama teaches a doctrine hammered out by reasoning, following his own line of inquiry, and based on his own ingenuity,” [they would speak falsely].
“Sāriputta, by not abandoning that speech, not abandoning that mind, and not relinquishing that view, one is placed in hell just as if carried there.
Sāriputta, just as a bhikkhu endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom might attain final knowledge in this very life;
even so, Sāriputta, do I say that by not abandoning that speech, not abandoning that mind, and not relinquishing that view, one is placed in hell just as if carried there.”
“Furthermore, Sāriputta, I recall practicing the holy life endowed with four factors.
I was indeed an ascetic, a supreme ascetic; I was indeed austere, supremely austere; I was indeed loathsome, supremely loathsome; I was indeed secluded, supremely secluded.

In that regard, Sāriputta, this was my asceticism: I went naked, rejecting conventions, licking my hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked; I did not accept food brought to me, nor food specially prepared for me, nor an invitation.”
Therefore, I do not accept [food] from the mouth of a jar, nor from the mouth of a basket;

not when a sheep is between [me and the giver], nor when a staff is between, nor when a pestle is between; not from two people eating together, nor from a pregnant woman, nor from a woman nursing, nor from a woman in the presence of her husband, nor from groups, nor where a dog is waiting, nor where flies are swarming.
Moving about in groups, I do not eat fish, nor meat, nor drink fermented liquor, nor spirits, nor grain-beer.

I am one who visits a single house for alms, or one who eats a single mouthful; or I am one who visits two houses for alms, or eats two mouthfuls... [and so on] ...or I am one who visits seven houses for alms, or eats seven mouthfuls.
I subsist on a single gift, or I subsist on two gifts... [and so on] ...or I subsist on as many as seven gifts.

I take food once a day, or I take food once every two days... [and so on] ...or I take food once every seven days; thus, in such a manner, I dwell devoted to the practice of taking meals at intervals, even for as long as half a month.

I become one who eats greens, or I become one who eats millet, or I become one who eats wild rice, or I become one who eats the *daddula* grain, or I become one who eats *haṭa* grass, or I become one who eats husks, or I become one who eats rice-scum, or I become one who eats oil-cake.
I become one who eats grass, or I become one who eats cow dung, or I subsist on forest roots and fruits, eating only what has fallen of its own accord.
I wear garments of hemp, or I wear garments of flax, or I wear shrouds from a cemetery, or I wear rag-robes, or I wear bark from the *tirīṭa* tree,
or I wear an antelope skin, or I wear a strip of antelope skin, or I wear a garment made of kusa grass.
I wear garments of bark, I wear garments of wood-shavings, I wear a blanket of human hair, I wear a blanket of animal fur,
and I wear an owl’s wing-feathers;
I am one who plucks out my hair and beard, devoted to the practice of plucking out my hair and beard.
I am one who stands continuously, rejecting seats;
I am one who squats, devoted to the exertion of squatting;
I am one who uses a bed of thorns, spreading my bed upon a layer of thorns.
I dwelt devoted to the practice of descending into water for the third time at night—
thus, in such ways, I dwelt devoted to many kinds of practices involving the mortification and tormenting of the body.
This, Sāriputta, was my asceticism.
In this regard, Sāriputta, I had this coarse appearance:
for many years, dust and dirt had accumulated on my body until it was cracked and flaked off.

Just as, Sāriputta, a tinduka stump that has stood for many years becomes covered with accumulated crust and cracks, even so, Sāriputta, dust and dirt had accumulated on my body for many years until it was cracked and flaked off.
“Sāriputta, it does not occur to me:
‘O, that I might wipe away this dust and dirt with my hand, or that others might wipe away this dust and dirt from me with their hands.
Even this, Sāriputta, does not occur to me.”
This, Sāriputta, was my coarse [food].
Therein, Sāriputta, this was my sense of revulsion:
I would approach and depart with mindfulness, and even toward a drop of water, compassion was established in me, thinking: [“May no harm come to this living being”].”
‘May I not bring about the destruction of small living beings that have come into my path.
This, Sāriputta, was what I felt as loathsome.
And herein, Sāriputta, this was what I felt as secluded:
So, Sāriputta, having entered a certain forest region, I dwelt there.

Whenever I saw a cowherd, a shepherd, a grass-gatherer, a wood-gatherer, or a forest-worker, I would go from forest to forest, from thicket to thicket, from low ground to low ground, and from high ground to high ground.
For what reason?
"May they not see me, and may I not see them.
Just as, Sāriputta, a forest deer, upon seeing humans, flees from wood to wood, from thicket to thicket, from low ground to low ground, and from high ground to high ground;
even so, Sāriputta, whenever I see a cowherd, a shepherd, or a grass-gatherer..."
Or [I see] one carrying firewood or one working in the forest, going from forest to forest, from thicket to thicket, from low ground to low ground,
or from high ground to high ground.
For what reason?
"May they not see me, and may I not see them.
This, Sāriputta, was my sense of seclusion.

Then, Sāriputta, I would go to those pastures where the cattle had been driven off and were without a cowherd; there, squatting on my haunches, I would eat the dung of the young calves that were still suckling at their mothers' teats.
"As long as my own urine and excrement were not yet exhausted, Sāriputta, I subsisted on my own urine and excrement.
This, Sāriputta, was my food among the great repulsive foods.
Then, Sāriputta, I would enter a certain terrifying forest thicket and dwell there."
In that regard, Sāriputta, there was this terrifying quality about that fearsome forest grove:
whenever anyone who was not free from lust entered that grove, their body hairs would mostly stand on end.
Therefore, Sāriputta, during those cold winter nights—the intervals between the eighth days when snow falls—I would dwell in the open air at night and in the forest grove by day.
In the last month of summer, Sāriputta, I dwell by day in the open air and by night in the forest grove.
And then, Sāriputta, this verse—never heard before—occurred to me spontaneously:
“Thirsting and parched with thirst, I am consumed by heat;”
‘The sage, alone in the terrifying forest,
naked and not sitting by a fire,
is intent on his quest.’”
Thus, Sāriputta, I made my bed in the charnel ground with the bones of the dead as my pillow.
And there, Sāriputta, village boys would come up to me, spit on me, urinate on me, throw dirt on me, and even thrust sticks into my ear canals.
Yet, Sāriputta, I do not recall ever having given rise to an evil thought toward them.
This, Sāriputta, was my dwelling in equanimity.
However, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
‘Purification comes through food.’
They said to him:
“Let us subsist on jujube fruits.
So they ate jujube fruits, they ate jujube powder, and they drank jujube water.
They consume various kinds of jujube preparations.
However, Sāriputta, I recall having consumed only a single jujube as food.
It might occur to you, Sāriputta, that:
‘At that time, Kola must surely have been great indeed.
But, Sāriputta, you should not view it in this way.
Even then, Kola was limited to exactly what he is now.
Sāriputta, as I was consuming only a single jujube fruit as food, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation.
Just as the joints of a withered creeper or a black vine, so did my limbs become through that very lack of food.
Just like a camel’s hoof, so did my buttocks become through that very lack of food.
Just as if it were a string of beads, even so my spine appeared with its vertebrae protruding one after another because of that very lack of food.
Just as if in an old shed the rafters were sagging and collapsing, even so my ribs were sagging and collapsing because of that very lack of food.

Just as if in a deep well the reflections of the stars seen in the water appear far down and sunken, even so the pupils in my eye-sockets appeared far down and sunken because of that very lack of food.
"Just as a bitter gourd, cut while raw, becomes withered and shriveled by the wind and sun, even so, Sāriputta, my skin on the head became withered and shriveled because of that very lack of food.
Then, Sāriputta, when I thought, 'I will touch the skin of my belly,' I instead grasped my backbone;
and when I thought, 'I will touch my backbone,' I instead grasped the skin of my belly. To such an extent, Sāriputta,"
The skin of my belly was so stuck to my backbone because of that very meagreness of food.
Indeed, Sāriputta, when I intended to defecate or urinate, I would fall right there on my face because of that very meagreness of food.

And, Sāriputta, while trying to comfort that body, I would rub my limbs with my hand; as I rubbed my limbs with my hand, Sāriputta, the hair fell from my body by its rotten roots because of that very meagreness of food.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as this:
‘Purification comes through food.
They speak thus:
‘We shall subsist on mung beans...
[and so on] ...we shall subsist on sesame seeds...
[and so on] ...we shall subsist on rice.’
They eat rice, they eat rice powder, they drink rice water—
they consume various kinds of rice preparations.
Yet, Sāriputta, I recall having taken only a single grain of rice as food.
It might occur to you, Sāriputta,
‘At that time Taṇḍula must surely have been a great man.
But, Sāriputta, it should not be viewed in this way.
Even then, Sāriputta, that grain was of the very same quality as it is now.
While I was consuming only a single grain of rice as my food, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation.
Just like the joints of an old bamboo stalk or a black bamboo stalk, so too did my limbs become through that very lack of food.
Just as the foot of an iguana, so too did my buttocks become like that because of that very lack of food.
Just as a string of beads, so too did my spine appear with its vertebrae protruding one after another because of that very lack of food.
Just as the rafters of a dilapidated old shed become sagging and decayed, so too did my ribs become sagging and decayed because of that very lack of food.
Just as in a deep well the reflections of the stars appear deep down, hanging suspended, even so in my eye-sockets the pupils appeared deep down, hanging suspended, because of that very lack of food.
Just as a bitter gourd, cut while raw, becomes withered and shriveled by the wind and sun, even so my scalp became withered and shriveled because of that very lack of food.
Thus, Sāriputta, thinking, “I will touch the skin of my belly,” I would grasp only my backbone;
thinking, “I will touch my backbone,” I would grasp only the skin of my belly. Indeed, Sāriputta, through that very lack of food, the skin of my belly clung to my backbone.
Thus, Sāriputta, thinking, "I shall defecate or urinate," I would fall right there face down because of that very meagreness of food.

Then, Sāriputta, seeking to comfort that body, I would rub my limbs with my hand. As I rubbed my limbs with my hand, Sāriputta, the hairs fell from my body by their very roots because of that very meagreness of food.
Yet, Sāriputta, by that conduct, by that practice, and by those ascetic feats, I did not attain any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
Why was that? Because I had not attained this noble wisdom—which is noble, leading out, and which leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as this:
‘Purification comes through the cycle of rebirth.
But, Sāriputta, that cycle of rebirth which has not been traversed by me during this long period of time is not easily found, except for the gods of the Pure Abodes.
“Sāriputta, were I to transmigrate among the gods of the Pure Abodes, I would not return again to this world.
Yet, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
‘Purity comes through rebirth.’”
Moreover, Sāriputta, there is no rebirth so easily obtained that I have not already undergone it during this long stretch of time, with the exception of the Suddhāvāsa deities.
And were I, Sāriputta, to be reborn among the Suddhāvāsa deities, I would not return again to this world.
Now, Sāriputta, there are some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
‘Purity by means of a dwelling.
Yet, Sāriputta, there is no such dwelling easily found that I have not already inhabited during this long period of time, except for the Suddhāvāsa deities.
And, Sāriputta, were I to dwell among the Suddhāvāsa deities, I would not return again to this world.
“Furthermore, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view:
‘Purification comes through sacrifice.

Yet, Sāriputta, such a sacrifice as has never been offered by me during this long interval is not easily found; it is only one offered by a consecrated head-anointed kṣatriya king or by a wealthy brahmin.”
Furthermore, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as this:
"Purification comes through the tending of the sacrificial fire.

Yet, Sāriputta, that fire which has not previously been tended by me during this long period of time is not easily found; it can only be obtained by a consecrated Khattiya king or by a wealthy Brahmin.
“Furthermore, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this doctrine and view:
‘As long as this person is young, a youth with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, so long is he possessed of the highest proficiency of wisdom.

But when this person becomes old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life—being eighty, ninety, or a hundred years from birth—then he declines from that proficiency of wisdom.’”
But this, Sāriputta, should not be viewed in such a way.
For I, Sāriputta, am now old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the end of my journey; my age has reached eighty.

Suppose, Sāriputta, I had four disciples here who were one hundred years of age, living for a hundred years, and endowed with supreme mindfulness, intelligence, and fortitude, as well as with the highest clarity of wisdom.
"Just as, Sāriputta, a firm-bowed archer— trained, practiced, and skilled— might with a light arrow effortlessly shoot through the shadow of a palm tree across the way;
even so, those who possess such supreme mindfulness, such supreme comprehension, and such supreme steadfastness, and who are endowed with the highest lucidity of wisdom—
if they were to question me again and again regarding each of the four foundations of mindfulness, I, being questioned, [would answer them]."
I would explain it to them, and they would remember what was explained by me as having been explained; they would not question me further for a second time.
Apart from eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; apart from the business of defecation and urination;
and apart from dispelling drowsiness and fatigue—Sāriputta, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma would remain unfinished, and the Tathāgata’s [life] would likewise remain unfinished.
The phrasing of the Dhamma-pada remains unexhausted, for the Tathāgata’s inspired response to questions is inexhaustible.
Suppose, Sāriputta, those four disciples of mine—each having a lifespan of a hundred years and living for a hundred years—were to pass away at the end of that hundred years.
Even if you were to carry me about on a bed, Sāriputta, there would still be no alteration in the clarity of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
“Sāriputta, if one were speaking rightly, it is of me that one would rightly say:

‘A being who is by nature free from delusion has arisen in the world for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.’”
Now at that time, the Venerable Nāgasamāla was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him.
Then the Venerable Nāgasamāla said this to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!”
“Indeed, Bhante, my hair stood on end upon hearing this discourse on the Dhamma.
What is the name, Bhante, of this discourse on the Dhamma?
“Therefore, Nāgasamāla, you should remember this discourse on the Dhamma as ‘The Hair-Raising Discourse.’”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Nāgasamāla, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, the second, is finished.
